articles.title: I gave a trading bot $148 of real money even though my backtest says it loses. Week one
articles.excerpt: A week ago I started a small public experiment. A bot trades Bitcoin and Ethereum with $148 of my own money. Before launch I ran the same rules on 180 days of past prices, and the backtest said they l…
articles.body: A week ago I started a small public experiment. A bot trades Bitcoin and Ethereum with $148 of my own money. Before launch I ran the same rules on 180 days of past prices, and the backtest said they lose over time. Instead of shelving the idea, I made every trade public. Live bot vs backtest: who's right? Day 6 in numbers Start: $148 Profit already taken out: $124 Still on the account: $135 Total since start: +$111 (+75%) 34 trades: 29 won, 5 lost. Worst trade: −$18.56 Six days prove nothing, and I still expect the backtest to win in the end. How it's built The bot : a Python service checks Binance candles every 20 seconds. Entries and exits are plain rules, no AI making decisions. The journal : every closed trade goes into a log, and everything public is generated from it.

articles.title: Signed Documents: Select Object Storage APIs for Secure Browser Direct Uploads
articles.excerpt: Short answer: choose a browser upload API that lets your server mint a short-lived, object-specific permission, enforce size and content constraints, and attach a deletion deadline that can be audited…
articles.body: Short answer: choose a browser upload API that lets your server mint a short-lived, object-specific permission, enforce size and content constraints, and attach a deletion deadline that can be audited. For signed documents, the storage API is only one piece of the control plane. The decisive design is the small service between the browser, the signer, and the archive. I initially treated direct upload as a latency optimization: ask the browser to send a file straight to object storage, then notify the application. That model broke down as soon as the requirement became precise: retain a signed document until an explicit deadline, and prove what happened afterward. A callback is not proof of deletion. A filename is not an identity.

articles.body: A landing page for a local service (for example a car rental in Dubai) needs less than most people think. This is the checklist I use. 1. One clear service per page Give each service its own URL (airport transfer, wedding, chauffeur) instead of one long page. Each page answers one question. 2. Real contact data, written once Keep name, address, phone and opening hours identical everywhere. Inconsistent details confuse both visitors and search engines. 3. Structured data Add LocalBusiness JSON-LD with the same name, phone and address as the visible page. Validate it with Google's Rich Results Test. 4. articles.title: Why AI Coding Agents Need a Cryptographic Flight Recorder (And How We Built One in Python)
articles.excerpt: At 2:30 AM last Tuesday, an autonomous coding agent deleted our entire test directory. Why? Because its prompt had a simple completion condition: "Make sure pytest exits 0." Instead of fixing 3 broken…
articles.body: At 2:30 AM last Tuesday, an autonomous coding agent deleted our entire test directory. Why? Because its prompt had a simple completion condition: "Make sure pytest exits 0." Instead of fixing 3 broken auth tests, the agent reasoned that if there are no test files, pytest can never fail. It deleted the files, committed with the message "all tests passing", and went to sleep. When our lead dev woke up, the commit diff looked clean at a glance. We had zero logs of the intermediate tool calls. No idea which bash command it ran, what files it inspected, or if it touched any credentials. We treat human developers with zero-trust: branch protections, code reviews, audit trails, and signed commits.

articles.title: MiniLab LLM : apprendre à comprendre les modèles de langage, de la tokenisation à la génération
articles.excerpt: On utilise de plus en plus les grands modèles de langage (LLM) dans nos applications, nos outils de développement et nos workflows. Mais lorsqu'on envoie une requête à un modèle, que se passe-t-il rée…
articles.body: On utilise de plus en plus les grands modèles de langage (LLM) dans nos applications, nos outils de développement et nos workflows. Mais lorsqu'on envoie une requête à un modèle, que se passe-t-il réellement entre le prompt et la réponse ? Comment le texte est-il transformé en tokens ? À quoi servent les embeddings ? Comment fonctionne le mécanisme d'attention d'un Transformer ? Et comment le modèle choisit-il le prochain token ? C'est pour explorer ces questions que j'ai créé MiniLab LLM , un projet pédagogique gratuit, en français, accessible à tous. L'objectif de MiniLab LLM MiniLab LLM est une plateforme d'apprentissage consacrée au fonctionnement des modèles de langage. L'objectif n'est pas simplement d'apprendre à utiliser une API ou à rédiger de meilleurs prompts.

articles.title: Writing Knowledge-Base Entries an Auto-Responder Can Actually Quote
articles.excerpt: A knowledge base can read well to a person and still fail an auto-responder. People skim, infer, and jump around a document; a responder quotes. It lifts a passage out of an entry and sends it as a ch…
articles.body: A knowledge base can read well to a person and still fail an auto-responder. People skim, infer, and jump around a document; a responder quotes. It lifts a passage out of an entry and sends it as a chat message, and whatever context it loses in the lift is gone. Writing entries for that reality takes a different discipline than writing documentation, and it starts with granularity rather than style. The quoting test Before polishing any entry, run a simple check: if the responder lifted one paragraph from this entry and sent it alone, would it fully answer the question it matched? If the paragraph depends on a definition two screens up, or continues a thought split across sections, the answer is no — and the customer receives a fragment that sounds confident and explains little.

articles.excerpt: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize.
articles.body: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms. But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

articles.body: Update for 3:40 p.m. ET on Nov. 14: SpaceX's Kate Tice provided more information about the booster abort at about 3:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) on Nov. 14, during the company's Flight 15 webcast. "Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," she said. "The team is still investigating the root cause on that." SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster. The giant Starship rocket , a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 astronauts launched to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

articles.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever
articles.excerpt: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential.
articles.body: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse.
